The House resumed from Monday, April 21, consideration of the motion of Miss MacDonald (Minister of Employment and Immigration), that Bill C-62, an Act respecting employment equity, be read the third time and passed; and on the amendment (Ms. Copps) (p. 12465).

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in this important debate at the third reading stage of the employment equity legislation known as Bill C-62. In effect, this Bill represents yet another broken promise of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney). Canadians will recall that throughout the 1984 election campaign the Prime Minister set out an ambitious program to implement full employment equity for all Canadians. I remind those Canadians who are watching the debate, and those who have been following it, of the words of the Prime Minister who said in August of 1984:
Our party will ensure that companies providing services to the federal Government hire increasing numbers of women to perform such services. When seeking Government business, these companies will be required to detail their action plans, timetables, and programs for attracting, training and advancing women within their operations-
The Prime Minister went on to say this:
We support the need for human resources planning within the federal bureaucracy, which includes goals and objectives to achieve parity for women, at all levels of Government operations, commensurate with their skills and expectations. Numerical goals are one of several goals required: training and retraining are others.
Canadians remember the promises made by the Prime Minister during the federal election campaign. Today, as we examine this legislation on employment equity, it is clear that those promises have been broken. In particular, the flaws in Bill C-62 are the promises which have been broken at the expense of groups in our society which have been historically disadvantaged when it comes to achieving equal access to labour market opportunities. In particular I speak of the disabled, of women, native people and visible minorities, all of whom had high hopes that the Tory Government would back up the rhetoric of the Prime Minister with concrete action.
That was not to be. Why is it that legislation such as effective employment equity legislation is so important? Time and time again we have had statistical studies, many of them referred to in the report of the Royal Commission on Equality and Employment, chaired so ably by Judge Rosalie Abella,

April 22, 1986
Employment Equity
that provide a very bleak picture indeed of the employment opportunities and benefits for designated groups. There is an imbalance in both statistical and monetary terms. Women have lower than average incomes. They are employed predominantly in sectors and in jobs which are the lowest paid. Women do not earn the same amount as their male counterparts for performing the same or similar jobs. Disabled people suffer from extraordinarily high unemployment rates. When they are employed they tend to be concentrated in the low-paying, marginal sectors of the labour market. They have additional expenses which those workers who are not disabled do not face, such as medication, special aids and devices, and special transportation services. Native people have incredibly high levels of unemployment, something in the order of five times higher than the non-native population. Recent immigrants to Canada face particular difficulties in advancing in the workforce. They are frequently found in job ghettos or in the lowest paid, lowest skilled and most vulnerable sectors of the employment market. So there is a problem which should have been addressed by the Government in its employment euqity legislation.
I spent some three months touring the country with the Subcommittee on Equality Rights. We travelled from coast to coast to hold public hearings. We heard representations from Canadians representing women's organizations, native people, the disabled and visible minorities. They expressed their very serious concerns about the provisions of Bill C-62.
I wish to take this opportunity to remind the House and, through the House, Canadians, of some of the concerns which have been raised regarding the legislation we are debating today. One of the key spokespersons for the disabled, Beryl Potter, of the Coalition on Employment Equity for Persons with Disabilities, said this:
Like the bill-it's not even worth the paper it's written on-I've never been so disillusioned in my life as I am with Prime Minister Mulroney. I was a supporter of him. I worked for him in his campaign and I am totally, totally disillusioned.
That from a former active Conservative and one of the heads of the Coalition on Employment Equity for Persons with Disabilities. The spokesperson for the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada said: "Bill C-62 is of limited value". The spokesperson of the National Association of Women and the Law, Suzanne Boivin, said:
Nothing will change. Unfortunately, it is simply wishful thinking.
The groups which are affected by this legislation are unanimous in their condemnation of it. At the end of the day it is clear that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Ms. MacDonald) and her Government have not effectively consulted with the groups affected by this legislation. In fact, they have ignored the major concerns raised by these groups and by their spokespeople.
I would like to take this opportunity to elaborate on why Bill C-62 is such a disappointment to the millions of Canadians who, in fact, were looking for concrete action, for decisive action, from the Government to ensure employment equity. First, I wish to recognize the excellent work done by Judge
Rosalie Abella in this area. We in the New Democratic Party have drawn upon her report in outlining what we believe to be the correct approach, the philosophical underpinnings of strong employment equity legislation. As well, I wish to underline the outstanding contribution made by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), who in his work both in committee and in the House has reflected with eloquence the concerns of the groups which appeared before the committee seeking changes to the legislation.
When we examine Bill C-62 we see that the purpose of the Bill as spelled out is certainly commendable. The purpose of the Bill, as stated, is as follows:
The purpose of this Act is to achieve equality in the workplace so that no person shall be denied employment opportunities or benefits for reasons unrelated to ability and, in the fulfilment of that goal, to correct the conditions of disadvantage in employment experienced by women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and persons who are, because of their race or colour, in a visible minority in Canada by giving effect to the principle that employment equity means more than treating persons in the same way but also requires special measures and the accommodation of differences.
That is the guiding principle of this legislation. However, when we go on to read the Bill itself, we find that it falls far short of that.
Once again, I would note that consultation with the groups affected by this legislation was sorely lacking. Beryl Potter, a former active supporter of the Conservative Party who now says that she has been betrayed by the Prime Minister of this country has said the following:
We have tried everything. We have consulted with the CEIC staff, appeared as witnesses before the Parliamentary Committee on the Bill, made pleas to the Prime Minister directly and rallied on Parliament Hill.
We have demanded that the Bill be amended to include the Government's own Departments and agencies and to include a penalty for failing to comply with employment equity plans. The Government has not responded to any of our demands.
All Hon. Members will recall that a week ago yesterday the members of the Coalition on Employment Equity for Persons with Disabilities came to Parliament Hill and sat in the gallery. In many cases, these people were lifted into the gallery. They were bitterly disappointed with the response of the Government.
We have five underlying concerns with respect to the weaknesses in this legislation and I would like to deal with each of them in turn. The first and perhaps most fundamental concern is with respect to the lack of any effective enforcement mechanism or penalties large enough to act as a deterrent to the corporate sector. Shari Stein, the legal counsel for the Coalition on Employment Equity for Persons with Disabilities, has said the following about Bill C-62:
How can anyone, the people, the provinces, the municipal Governments, take this legislation seriously when it has no teeth, it only requires voluntary compliance and the federal Government has exempted itself.
Furthermore, the Bill does not require that the so-called action plans with goals and timetables established by the firms be made available to the Human Rights Commission or the
April 22, 1986

Canadian Employment and Immigration Commission. In effect, there is no mechanism whatsoever to guard against plans which may be poorly devised and wholly inadequate to meet the needs of target groups. We have examined the response of the Government to the unanimous recommendations of the equality committee.
I see that the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock- North Delta (Mr. Friesen) is present in the House. I know how strongly he supported the recommendations of the committee on equality and I know that he will want to have a chance to speak on that at the appropriate time. The committee recommended far more effective legislation. It recommended that the Government give teeth to Bill C-62 and ensure that there are adequate employment equity enforcement mechanisms. Those mechanisms are not there and I deeply regret that. Certainly the groups affected by this Bill regret that very much.
The Bill makes no reference whatsoever to equal pay for work of equal value. Here both Judge Abella and the National Action Committee on the Status of Women recommended that concrete and specific reference should be made to the important principle of equal pay for work of equal value and that it should be included in the legislation itself.
As well, there are no provisions for mandatory contract compliance for firms which may be doing business with the Government. Clearly the experience in the United States has shown that contract compliance can be a very effective tool in changing discriminatory practices which may be followed by firms selling goods and services to the Government. This was a major recommendation of the Equality for All report and the Government has chosen to ignore it.
The Abella Commission's recommendation No. 27 states that contract compliance should be imposed by legislation. The Government has ignored that important recommendation. In Bill C-62, we see that contract compliance only applies to firms with 100 or more employees and only if the value of the contracts exceed $200,000. Moreover, failure to comply with the equity proposals of the Government does not result in loss of a contract but only means that in the future, such a firm may be removed from competition. That is not much of an incentive to comply with employment equity. I know that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) has fought a vigorous battle within Cabinet to strengthen this Bill but unfortunately was beaten back by the right wing of the Tory Cabinet and caucus.
The provisions with respect to employment equity and in particular contract compliance are set out in the report entitled Equality for All. The unanimous recommendation of the committee composed of five Conservative Members, one Liberal Member and myself was that contract compliance be a part of the employment equity legislation. We noted that in the United States, a similar executive order enforced by the office of federal contract compliance programs applies to contracts worth $50,000 or more granted to firms with 50 or more employees. The unanimous recommendation of our committee was that the ceiling of $200,000 and 100 employees
Employment Equity
is too high. That was a recommendation made unanimously by the committee with respect to this legislation that is now before the House. I know that some Hon. Members from the other side of the House fought for this but obviously lost out.
There were recommendations in other areas about which the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta felt particularly strongly. I know that he fought hard in those areas. However, the reality is that that particular voice was not heard, and in some instances, perhaps we might breathe a sigh of relief that that was the case. However, I know that the Hon. Member himself may wish to comment with respect to his views on this important report.
Much of the wording of Bill C-62, particularly that of Clause 4 which deals with the duty of employers, is very loose and ill defined. What, for example, is the effect of not defining reasonable accommodation or positive policies and practices? This crucial question should surely be the subject of negotiation between employers and employees. Instead, there has been some vague process of consultation and even that was only included as an amendment later in the day.
Finally, the fifth major concern we have with respect to this Bill is that federal Government departments including the RCMP and the Canadian armed forces must be included within the scope of the legislation. Once again, this was a recommendation made very clearly by the special committee on equality rights. We said that the legislation on employment equity should apply to all federal public-sector employers and to employers under federal jurisdiction. Despite that unanimous recommendation, the Government once again told us to forget it, that it is not prepared to implement that important recommendation.
I think we can understand why the Government did that if we read an extract from the Government's response. The Government has said that it attempts to balance the needs of the designated groups against the Government's desire not to interfere unduly in the operations of employers. It is a pretty skewed balance and one which has left the groups which should be assisted by employment equity legislation, women, native people, the disabled and visible minorities, very critical indeed of the legislation.
The Government argued that federal Departments and agencies are covered by the 1983 Public Service policy on affirmative action. I would remind the Government that that policy does not apply to members of the RCMP or the armed forces. We know that those employers are some of the most reactionary and sexist employers in the country. We hoped that they would have been included under this legislation, weak though it may be.
I would like to conclude by reminding the House once again that during the 1984 federal election campaign, Conservative Members raised the expectations of groups which had historically been disadvantaged, groups which had hoped that the Government's promises would be kept. Rather than that,

April 22, 1986
Employment Equity
we see a legacy of broken promises in so many other areas as well as in this fundamental area of social justice.
These groups had hoped that corrective action would be taken to deal with past abuses and ongoing barriers to workplace equity. They also recognized that the previous Government took no action whatsoever, and certainly they were critical of the former Government for its failure to act. It is interesting to see the spokesperson for that Party now standing up in opposition and railing at the Government in respect of action which should have been taken many years ago. Certainly many of us who were here when Liberal Governments were in power were critical of their inaction. We hoped that the Tories would keep their promises.
Instead of providing mechanisms in the Bill to ensure compliance through effective enforcement, Bill C-62 relies on voluntarism and invitations. Surely the past has shown us clearly that it is not good enough to leave it to employers to establish and pursue their own goals and targets. The Minister somehow believes that if the failure of employers to live up to these goals and timetables is published, employers will be shamed into action. The record of employers across the land is well known and has been clearly documented. Certainly they have not been shamed into taking steps which would involve the full participation of all Canadians in the workforce.
As the New Democratic Party understands it-and this is understood by millions of women, native people, disabled persons, and visible minorities-employment equity requires a solid commitment to using the instruments of Government to ensure that ideals become reality. We need enforcement mechanisms with teeth. We need provisions for contract compliance, negotiation between management and workers, and a clearly stated commitment to the overriding principle of equal pay for work of equal value. Those essential principles are lacking in this important piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member knows that the Opposition, both in committee and at report stage in the House, tried to amend Clause 7 of the Bill, that is the clause dealing with penalties. We tried to amend it so that the penalty would apply not only to employers who failed to comply with section 6 but also to employers who failed to comply with Clauses 4 and 5. While Clause 4 obliges employers to implement employment equity, the Hon. Member knows that there is no penalty in the Bill if they do not comply with it. Also, Clause 5 obliges employers to prepare an action plan with goals and timetables, but there is no penalty for non-compliance. Both his Party and my Party proposed an amendment to Clause 7 which read that if an employer failed to comply with Clauses Nos. 4, 5, and 6 they would be guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding $500,000, and it was turned down by the Government.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) is a learned attorney, and I should like his views on the argument given by the Government. The Government said that it was not
necessary to make Clause 7 apply to Clauses 4 and 5 because by referring the reports under section 6 to the Canadian Human Rights Commission, Clauses 4 and 5 could be enforced under the Canadian Human Rights Act. I am a lawyer as well. I have read that Act from beginning to end and from end to beginning. In any case, I cannot follow the argumentation of the Government. If it were really in favour of enforcement, why would it not accept that simple amendment to Clause 7? I ask the Hon. Member, who is known to be a competent attorney, whether he has examined those arguments of the Government, which I failed to grasp, indicating that the Bill did not require an enforcement clause because the Canadian Human Rights Act would take care of that.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my distinguished colleague and learned legal associate for his important question. I am not at all surprised that the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) has failed to comprehend the Government's reasoning. Indeed, all reasonable Canadians and all groups affected by the legislation do not understand the Government's reasoning.
The Bill is very specific. Only Clause 7 is specifically an offence section. It reads:
An employer who fails to comply with section 6 is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding $50,000.
Certainly an employer who fails to comply with Clause 5, the one dealing with so-called action plans or the amendment which was added in committee, or with Clause 4, the one dealing with the employer's general duty to promote employment equity, would be able to say that there was no provision in the law for mandatory compliance with those clauses. Clause 7 only deals with the failure to comply with Section 6. It is quite clear that by singling out one section for the purposes of enforcement and deliberately not making references to the two clauses which are at the heart of the Bill in real terms, the Government is saying to the corporate sector: "Please comply. This is what we would like you to do, but if you are not prepared to do it, we are not prepared to enforce it". It is certainly a betrayal of the hopes and expectations of the groups affected.
In response to the suggestion that the Canadian Human Rights Act would somehow give the Canadian Human Rights Commission the opportunity to enforce these clauses, I searched that Act, as did my colleague, and there was absolutely no provision for that. We could obtain a learned legal opinion from the Chief Law Officer of the Crown who is present in the Chamber today, the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada. He might want to point to a section in the Canadian Human Rights Act which would give the Commission the power in fact to enforce these clauses or to put teeth into them. I do not want to take up any more time because I want to give the Minister of Justice an opportunity to clarify for all Canadians just how the Canadian Human Rights Commission will have the opportunity to enforce these clauses.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with the position taken by the Hon. Member with regard to the enforcement policies and provisions in Bill C-62. As reported at page 12454 of Hansard for yesterday, the Minister made the following statement:
The Government is committed to ensuring that employment equity becomes a reality. We intend to knock on the doors of employers who do not meet their responsibilities. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that we will be knocking with a firm fist.
That confirms exactly what we have been saying. The Government only has pious hopes but no way of enforcing them, because there is no obligation on any employer to report progress. Would the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) tell us how he thinks the Minister will be able to knock on the doors of employers with a firm fist? What kind of a result does he think the Minister will get? What about an employer who says: "I will not tell you the progress I am making on employment equity because it is none of your business; the law does not force me to do that"? How does he foresee the reaction of a medium sized employer with 100 or more employees? Of course employers will be required to fulfil a couple of obligations. They will have to plan for eliminating systemic discrimination and presenting a plan of action. However, I do not see anything in the Bill that forces them to report on progress made. Can the Hon. Member find anything in the Bill requiring progress made being reported to the Canadian Human Rights Commission?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa- Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) quite correctly pointed out one of the very serious weaknesses in the legislation. There is no real clout in the hands of the Minister to enforce the legislation. All she can do is get down on bended knee and beg, plead, cajole, request, and urge. All she can do is knock on the door and say: "Please, Mr. Employer, hire more disabled persons and more women". That approach has been tried in the past for decades, and it has not worked.
When we in the New Democratic Party looked at the legislation, we worked hard to strengthen the Bill. Hon. Members of the Official Opposition also proposed amendments which would put some teeth into it. When the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier talks about the Minister knocking on the doors of employers and insisting upon action, what we will find instead is the Minister standing outside corporate boardrooms and whimpering: "Please, please, please, we want you to obey this law, and if you do not obey it, we might amend it". In the law itself there are no sanctions or teeth whatsoever.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will quote further from the Minister's speech of yesterday. It is quite interesting how a Minister of the Crown could make such statements. I will come back to this later on in my speech about this because I noticed some interesting comments of hers yesterday. At page 12453 of Hansard, the Minister said:
At the end of that year they will be required to report on the progress that they have made toward achieving these goals. These reports will be made public, open
Employment Equity
to media and public scrutiny-and this is the second half of the two-tiered system-
This is exactly what Judge Abella rejected, voluntary reporting on progress. She said that you cannot believe that public opinion will change an employer who has in his practices or has in his systemic employment practices actions discriminatory to the four groups we are talking about, namely, women, the handicapped, native peoples and visible minorities. If an employer has in his books or in his practices things that discriminate against these groups, how does the Member square what the Minister told us yesterday with the Abella Report which says: "Don't rely on voluntary reporting because it won't happen"? It has not happened yet and it will not start happening after Bill C-62 is passed.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has joined me today in this important debate. I would be quite prepared to seek unanimous consent to ask the Minister to answer that very important question.
Oh, oh!

In the short time available, I would note that the Hon. Member is raising a very important question. Under this legislation and, in particular, Clause 5 of the legislation it states that while an employer has to prepare a plan which sets out various goals and timetables, this plan remains a secret document. The employer has to keep it locked in his or her principal place of business for a period of at least three years, but the employer does not even have to give it to the Canadian Human Rights Commission. In committee, the opposition Party suggested that if we are going to be able to monitor effectively the progress of employers in achieving employment equity, we should at least make sure that we have access to the statement of the achievement of goals and timetables as recommended by Judge Abella. That amendment was rejected. For that, as well as the many other reasons that we have been enunciating during the course of this debate, we are opposed to the third reading of this Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. The Hon. Member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille).

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-62, an Act respecting, as it says, employment equity, is a Bill which has been the subject of debate in the House now for some period of time. We have to ask ourselves, does this Bill in third reading, after we have tried to work on amendments and ways to improve it, fulfil its declared purposes? The purpose as outlined in the Bill in the second clause, in about the third sentence, sets forth what the alleged purpose of this Bill is. It is to achieve equality in the workplace. It says: "In the workplace".
First, Mr. Speaker, it is only in some workplaces, it is not in "the workplace". In fact, we have to say that "the workplace" only applies to those workplaces where there are more than

April 22, 1986
Employment Equity
100 people employed, otherwise this Bill does not apply. Next, it does not apply to the entire private sector, only to a number of companies doing federal work. Further, it does not really apply to any federal Departments. It does not even apply to this House of Commons or to the other place, the Senate.
When we look at what it does apply to, we find that the Bill applies to some federal Crown corporations and about 800 federally regulated firms with more than 100 employees. Otherwise this Bill applies to no one else. It certainly does not apply in any way to "the workplace". It applies to only a very few workplaces in Canada. Therefore, from the beginning, the Bill is a sham in terms of its alleged purposes.
The Bill says that no person shall be denied employment. Clause 2 states:
The purpose of this Act is to achieve equality in the workplace so that no person shall be denied employment opportunities or benefits for reasons unrelated to ability and, in the fulfillment of that goal, to correct the conditions of disadvantage in employment experienced by women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities-
These are the people in the groups to which the Bill is supposed to apply and whom it is supposed to help. It says it is "to achieve equality". This Bill does not change a single solitary thing, Mr. Speaker. It does not change anything. It is supposed to attack systemic discrimination against certain groups. By systemic discrimination we mean the way the system works, the network, the basic underlying system as we know it, the ingrained system. Women know what this ingrained system is because they know that they have not achieved in any sense the positions of leadership and of power in any way equally to men.
The handicapped certainly know what the system is. They know in very many ways that they are regarded as useless instead of being regarded as excellent resources. Various minority groups, especially our native peoples, understand how the system works, but it does not work for them.
This Bill is suppose to change systemic discrimination. It is supposed to affect the system. It is a sham. The Bill is an absolute sham. Who says it is a sham, Mr. Speaker? I say it is a sham. The opposition Parties agree it is a sham.
In my work in the field of human rights, I have had some occasion over these months to talk to people in that field. There is not one single person who works in the field of human rights who does not regard the Bill as a sham.
If we look also at groups who are affected, at umbrella groups, because I would not want to read off the whole list of the names of the organizations that regard this Bill as a sham, let me just say briefly that the umbrella groups include the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, the Coalition of Provincial Organizations of the Handicapped, the Urban Alliance on Race Relations, the National Ethnocultural Council, the Canadian Association for Community Living, formerly the Canadian Association of the Mentally Retarded, the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Congress for Learning Opportunities for Women, and the Coalition on Employment Equity for Persons with Disabilities. That is not
the complete list. That is only a list of some of the umbrella groups. Hundreds and hundreds of leaders of groups across the country have spoken up and have written, and although they declare the Bill a sham, the Government persists in putting this Bill through unamended.
There have been certain comments that I think are worth putting on the record. For example, Carol Tator, President of the Urban Alliance on Race Relations, says:
What the government has done has given us an empty, symbolic gesture toward the whole problem of achieving employment equity.
Shari Stein, a lawyer for the Advocacy Resource Centre for the Handicapped, adds that Bill C-62 is so weak it is potentially harmful. That is why the Opposition is so determined. If this legislation moved a small step in the right direction, one would not feel that one had to fight this to get it changed drastically. However, when groups like this call this Bill harmful, one must listen, take notice, and realize that a lot is at stake.
The purpose of this Bill is allegedly to ensure that no person is denied employment opportunities or benefits. Those are high sounding ideals, but what does this Bill do for our minority groups? My colleagues, who have analysed this Bill as I have, have pointed out that, in effect, this Bill only asks employers to file a report. The terminology of the report is not laid out. We moved amendments to clarify some of the terms, but they were not supported by the Government. Only employers who have more than 100 employees and fall into limited categories are affected by this Bill. They have to file some reports. We asked how the Government would ensure that employers would have a plan for the future to change their employment practices. After fighting against it as hard as possible, the Government finally saw fit to require employers to prepare a plan setting out their goals and timetables. The Government said employers should fill their drawers with their plans and keep them for at least three years. They are not to send these plans to the Government or the Canadian Human Rights Commission, but only to fill their drawers with them.
It is ludicrous that the Government, in all sincerity, could present such a Bill as this which is mocked by the people whom it is supposed to serve. The Government persists in refusing all of the recommendations which have been made to it by the minority groups and in ignoring the very reports which were presumably the cause for bringing forth this legislation. The Government consulted with these groups, commissioned the Abella Report, and appointed a committee on equality, which included Conservative members and unanimously called for the inclusion of various rigorous provisions, none of which are to be found in this Bill.
The women of Canada comprise 51 per cent of our population. As a group, they earn lower salaries than men and perform a higher proportion of part-time work. Very often they are the last hired and the first fired. Due to their frequent part-time employment, they are in a situation of great vulnerability. Over the decades the system has not corrected
April 22, 1986

itself. We cannot accept the views of the Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) that, because she is an eternal optimist and has faith in the Canadian people, things will work out.
It is not a question of the Canadian people, in whom we all have faith. It is a question of the employers who have to make a profit. Some of these employers are good citizens. However, it is not the good citizens toward whom we direct legislation, but the bad ones. There is no guarantee in this Bill that the bad citizens, or let us say the more self-centred citizens, in the corporate field are going to understand that we mean business. The Parliament of Canada is not a place to play games, and we resent that the Government is playing games with an issue as serious as equality for such a large proportion of our population.
Surely no injustice can be tolerated simply on the grounds that its correction will cost money. The complaint that the extra work of filling out these forms might be a bit expensive will not be accepted by Canadians any more than we will accept the view that we should not bother to keep the environment clean, because it will cost companies money. Let us keep the environment clean and let us keep the workplace clean and free of inequality and discrimination. Today women are supporting themselves and their dependants. They are working for a living and for survival. They have the right to equal pay for work of equal value. They have the right to take their rightful role as equal human beings. That is what Canadians want from the Government.
We sometimes hear from the less progressive elements of the business community that women must be moved from low-paying jobs into higher paying jobs through affirmative action. That is a laudable thought, but who will then fill the low-paying jobs which are left vacant? The problem is that those jobs are undervalued. If they continue to be undervalued because women fill them, we will not have solved the problem.
The lot of women has not been corrected by time and the so-called goodwill which exists. Despite educational campaigns and efforts by women's groups, the situation still has not changed. The claim that when the public sees what corporations and companies are doing they will make them change their ways is a vain and silly proposal of the Tories. It is not enough to simply rely on so-called public opinion and pressure. There must be legal requirements backed up by penalties for violation. There must be penalties for lack of compliance. There must be an enforcement mechanism. We all know this is the case, yet the Government persists in ignoring these obvious requirements to make this Bill meaningful.
Women's groups condemn this legislation as a sham. They constitute 51 per cent of the population. They were promised action but received a Bill with no compliance or penalties. I would like to deal with each of the minority groups, but time does not permit it. Time does not permit me to explore the loss of dignity which results from inequality. These people want the right to work. They do not want to be on the dole.
Employment Equity
The reason a law with enforcement provisions is required is that very often, as Martin Luther King said, the law is a teacher. It helps to make all of us understand our role. I remember many, many years ago, about the time I was ordained, that a black priest came to Toronto from New York City. I tried to find him quarters in a motel or hotel near Toronto. I was told by the proprietors that they had nothing against him because they liked black people, but the trouble was that the people who came up from the States did not like black people. If there were a law, of course, they could point to it and say, "We have to do this". However, since there was no law, they could not comply and they felt it was best for their business that they did not provide this man with accommodations. I am not talking about the United States deep south; I am talking about an area in Ontario in the 1950s. Why am I telling this story? To point out that if people have something to point to and say, "I have to do this", it helps them to justify what they know they should do. This is what the law requires and this is what they will do.
We are talking about something which deals with making us all equal as brothers and sisters together. 1 think Archibald MacLeish summed that up when he was writing a poem about the astronauts when they were looking down from the moon upon the earth. He said: "To see ourselves as riders on the earth together, brothers on that bright loveliness in the eternal cold, brothers who now know they are truly brotherse", and one might say, sisters who now know they are truly sisters.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to a good presentation by the Hon. Member. He presents himself as an advocate for the end of discrimination against women. However, am I not correct in thinking that he is a member and supporter of a church which refuses to ordain women as bishops? Would he tell us why that is the case? Would he take this opportunity to stand in his place and tell us, if he is a man of conviction, that he thinks the church of which he is a member is wrong? Would he tell us, if he is a man of conviction, that the law he would have applied to Governments and businesses should also apply to churches, and end once and for all discrimination against women in the church of which he is a member, and also other churches who engage in the same discriminatory practices?
Repent!

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure whether the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) is advocating support for the churches in such a stand or whether he is criticizing it. Perhaps he wants to know what my particular stand is. I could point out to him that the position which has historically existed in the Anglican Church, to which I belong, has forbidden the idea of the ordination of women as priests or as bishops. That position has been modified, at least in the

April 22, 1986
Employment Equity
church in Canada, so that we ordain women as priests. I have certainly supported that move.
However, the argument put forward by those who are, if I may say, less progressive and more conservative, against ordaining women as bishops is that it will be a problem for us ecumenically in our relationships with other churches who do not ordain women as bishops. I think that argument is specious and reactionary. Therefore, I have to say to my hon. friend that I believe that the Anglican Church to which I belong should hastily reform its position and join the 20th century. I invite Conservative Members of Parliament to join the 20th century as well and see to it that women are given equality in all areas. There is no room for inequality in this day and age and certainly not in this country.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Eglinton- Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) is a member of a Party which formed the Government of this country for a good number of years. It lead us to the present circumstances in which, for example, there are very few women in senior management positions in the federal Public Service. His Government tolerated this situation while it was in office. It promulgated policies which did not change that situation. There was no contract compliance policy which worked. The Liberals did not force companies to take action on employment equity. I am wondering how he can stand up in this House and criticize the Conservatives for doing just what his Government did over a number of years.
Mr. Speaker, first I would disagree with my friend on his statement that the Liberal Government did not do anything.
Nothing effective.

I think he has to realize that a very large number of steps were taken, step by step, starting with the federal Human Rights Commission. Guidelines in this area were brought into existence, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms was brought forward. It provides the legal basis on which all of these equality approaches are based and to which they are tied. Then of course we brought forward guidelines in the Treasury Board and we took other steps in the Public Service.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), was trying to bring into legislation amendments which would make sure that government Departments fall under the requirements of this Bill. I certainly agree that more needs to be done. Following upon the establishment of Human Rights Commissions and the Charter, and Section 15 of the Charter, as well as following upon the guidelines, the Liberal Government appointed the Abella Commission in order to receive recommendations as to how the Charter and the law should be applied. The Charter was passed four years ago and there was plenty of time for this Government to know what was coming up. It has finally decided to turn to the Council on Social Development to deal
with providing money to people for court challenges. That organization sent a list of these people to my friend, the Secretary of State, but he has not acted on it. Seven months have gone by and these people, who have genuine problems to take to court, are still waiting for the Government to act.
It is problems such as that which make me so concerned that this Bill is a sham. We will see more reports like this, with greater bureaucracy, but no action.

Before I direct a question to my hon. friend, I want to suggest that no political Party, including the New Democratic Party, has much to be proud of in its past with respect to employment equity. After listening to some remarks yesterday, I looked at the record and found that in Saskatchewan where the NDP was in power for some time, there is no legislated mandatory affirmative action program. In Manitoba, they only passed a pay equity Act in June, 1985. That is the only measure of any consequence in the area of affirmative action. In British Columbia, where the New Democratic Party was in power for some time, there is no legislation at all dealing with this subject. I suggest that all of us have come to it a bit late and I would expect there would be some humility with respect to this subject.
The fact is that we did pass the Canadian Human Rights Act in 1977 and the Charter of Rights in the last Parliament.
Clause 4 of the Bill says that an employer shall implement employment equity by instituting such positive policies and practices and making such reasonable accommodation as will ensure that persons in designated groups achieve a degree of representation in the workplace. There is no definition of reasonable accommodation in the Bill. All of the groups representing the disabled told us that there must be a definition or the Bill will be ineffective. As a Member who deals with disabled people very often, will he elaborate on this, because the Government has refused to accept our proposals for a definition of reasonable accommodation? Does he believe that this Bill can be effective for disabled people when it does not include a definition of reasonable accommodation?

Mr. Speaker, obviously the disabled and their organizations felt that this was a very essential and important definition to put in the Bill. Otherwise, the danger is that a disabled person could be defined as someone who has a sprained thumb. That is an exaggeration, but unless there is a definition of "disabled" and of "reasonable accommodation", the Bill will not provide any teeth at all as far as the handicapped are concerned. There are no terms of reference on which the the Government or the Human Rights Commission can act. The absence of this definition makes the Bill even more faulty than it is.
The disabled who came here last week were disappointed that they could not find a place in the gallery for their wheelchairs. This very place is limited in its facilities for the disabled, yet we are supposed to be setting an example for the
April 22, 1986

rest of the country. They came here and tried to cry out in protest in front of the House. They tried, through the media, to ask for these small amendments in order to give them reassurance that the Bill dealt with this issue seriously. Yet they were refused.
Some of the disabled who came here were blind. They may have been blind but they can see better than the Tories. They can look through the Tories and see the cynicism and hypocrisy.
