The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss MacDonald (Minister of Employment and Immigration), that Bill C-62, An Act respecting employment equity, be read the third time and passed; and on the amendment (Ms. Copps) (p. 12465).

Mr. Speaker, although Bill C-62 is supposed to achieve employment equity, it fails to contain many of the necessary provisions to achieve that goal. In fact, it has so many shortcomings in its structure that we have fairly said that it should be called at best a Bill to promote and encourage employment equity.
I am taking part in a debate on a motion which would give the Government an opportunity to reconsider seriously the representations that have been made in the House as well as in many other places about the flaws in the Bill.
Employment Equity
First, I want to respond to the comment by the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) about how slowly we have come to understand these matters. That observation does have some fairness to it. The proclamation of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms has demonstrated a growing sensitivity to these matters. The Hon. Member commented on the western provinces that have been governed by the New Democratic Party. Saskatchewan does not have a New Democratic Government at this time and British Columbia, of course, has not had a New Democratic Government for more than a dozen years. In Manitoba, I am pleased to say that the New Democratic Government was recently re-elected and that Government has been very concerned about making progress in this area, particularly as far as its own employment is concerned.
Members should be aware that in its negotiations with the union of Government employees, the Government of Manitoba took action in areas which the federal Government has refused to include in this Bill.
The Manitoba New Democratic Government negotiated an arrangement with the union of Government employees by which the proportion of women, native people, disabled and visible minorities in Manitoban society will be reflected in the composition of Government employees over a period of time. This is not a statement of what is desirable or a declaration that sets a goal. It is an agreement that was made with the union of Government employees by which workers will join with the Government in achieving these changes. Provisions have been made so that over a period of some 20 years the Manitoban Public Service will take up the characteristics we would expect if we are really going to practise the employment equity that we want. Of course, Judge Rosalee Abella, in her royal commission report over a year ago, set this forth as the basis for affirmative action and social justice in our country.
I have been handed a note stating that the study conducted for the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) shows that the Saskatchewan New Democratic Government expected real affirmative action progress from the Crown corporations which it established in the province. I want to note one paragraph in particular. It states:
Another strategy that was adopted in Saskatchewan that has, in the first instance, produced some results, was the approach taken in relation to the provincial crown corporations. Under the former Government-
Presumably, this is a document from the present Saskatchewan Conservative Government which states:
Under the former Government, affirmative action encompassed special measures to eliminate systemic discrimination and to open up employment opportunities to the key target groups (native, women, disabled).
The crown corporations were given a specific directive from the provincial government to develop affirmative action plans. Native people were designated the priority, although both women and the disabled were included as target groups.
The paragraph concludes:
12544

April 22, 1986
Employment Equity
The crown corporations were to demonstrate leadership and to provide an example to the private sector of effective affirmative action programs.
I am sure that some of my colleagues from Saskatchewan will be aware of these matters, even if the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) was not. I am sure that the Parliamentary Secretary is keenly aware of what the New Democratic Party in Saskatchewan is doing to ensure that northern development and mining development will provide opportunities for native peoople and, through those actions, ensure that affirmative action is being practised.
Having said that about two of the western provinces in which New Democrats have governed, I would like to return to the subject before us. More particularly, I return to the proposal that Clauses 3, 5 and 7 of Bill C-62 be referred back to committee for further consideration. It seems to me that it is important to give this opportunity to the Government so that it can take another look at the matter. After all, initially, there were fine statements of intention. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) is nothing if not a most impressive speaker when it comes to stating fine intentions and putting them forward with a lovely smile on her face, making one think that all will be sunny in these particular areas.
That was not the case, however, when she was faced with the type of particulars seen in the City of Toronto. These were made obvious by a couple of reports last winter and spring which asked: "No discrimination here?" "Who gets the jobs?" It was clear that in the employment patterns of employers in the City of Toronto there was a pattern of discrimination in place against those who were regarded as alien in one way or another. Whether this came about because of race and colour, or whether it was a matter of accents or the names people bore, these persons had great difficulty in obtaining employment. They obtained far fewer job offers even though they had similar qualifications to persons who were white, who looked familiar and who spoke English as the mainstream of Canadians have learned to speak English. These demonstrations of discrimination and racist practices were certainly known to the Minister.
I made a point of writing to the Minister after each of these reports to say to her: "Here is the evidence. We require strong action. Are we going to get it?" Of course, she would reassure us. When she tabled Bill C-62 we were all concerned to see what was in it. Even on first reading of it we found it did not contain very much. We found that, primarily, it was a basis for determining what the composition of workforces in large companies would be. It was primarily large companies with which it dealt. Government Departments were not included. We were told that other action was supposedly being taken- again, government by press release. But the Government was not making itself subject to this reporting provision. Only large employers with 100 or more employees would be required to report on the composition of their workforces. That is all the Bill provides. Certainly, there is a penalty for not complying, but who will tell me that $50,000 is a large penalty for the type
of corporations with which we are dealing here? It is not much of a penalty and not much will result in the way of action by employers.
We can be pleased that the argument which took place in the House, the debate here and in committee, produced the inclusion of one clause which actually opened the door to some real expectations, not demands on employers. At least with the addition of Clause 5 we have the following statement:
An employer shall, in respect of each year, prepare a plan setting out
(a)	the goals that the employer intends to achieve in implementing
employment equity-
(b)	the timetable for the implementation of those goals.
However, there are weaknesses in this clause, as I will suggest in a few moments, following others which still do not go very far. Employers were not just expected to report on the results of their employment practices, they were to set goals. Nowhere in the addition to the legislation, in this limited improvement in the Bill, was there a statement with respect to the type of goals that Government and the Parliament of Canada would expect lawyers to follow. There was no demand, no setting of a timetable for real progress to be made. Again, this demonstrates that if the Government was responding to the barrage of criticism it was receiving with respect to this promotion of employment equity by the use of legislation, the response was still a very limited one.
Given the protests of group after group, there has been a real formation of coalitions to press the Government to give more. I underscore that point as it comes from the various groups across the country. If the Government does not do something now, then I am convinced that it will not do it in the life of its mandate which the electorate gave it in 1984. We will have to wait until the year 1990 before seeing anything in the way of stronger legislation. That makes it all the more imperative for the Government to take seriously its own statement of conviction and principle, the statements which have been uttered from one quarter after another to the effect that the Bill is inadequate. It must open up the possibility of looking at Clauses-and I will take them up in this order-7, 5 and 3 in order to strengthen the Bill so that the people of Canada have what they really want in the way of legislation which will achieve employment equity.
Clause 7 contains a provision for the levy of a fine. As I have already stated, the sanction here for employers who do not act on the provisions of the Bill apply only to the reporting provision. Surely, if Clause 5 means anything, if the formulation of plans with goals really amounts to something, then it makes sense that if employers are doing that then their action should be subject to a fine much larger than $50,000. Surely, sending the Bill back to committee in order to open up the possibility of adding to Clause 5 in such a way that employers will be under the onus of law to do something about it makes sense. It is surely necessary to open up the possibility of doing this for diverse employers. This will ensure that it is not only large employers employing more than 100 people who can so easily pay $50,000. The payment of a $50,000 fine could
April 22, 1986

become a mere business expense if an employer did not want to go to the other trouble. As a matter of fact, if we consider the money which might have to be spent in formulating plans, then surely $50,000 might end up being less than the cost of establishing an office of employment equity in a company. In fact, $50,000 would not buy that much time, if an employer has to have some skilled people working in the area. A fine less than the cost of following through with these measures is certainly tantamount to inviting a violation of the law.
These are some reasons for having the Government send this Bill back to committee and, in particular, to consider some significant additions to Clause 7 by way of an increase in the fine and an assurance that it would apply to more than simply the filing of reports.
Clause 5, the clause to which I was just alluding, ensures that employers do not simply report on their employment practices but actually implement plans. Surely if the Government is serious about achieving employment equity as it declares on the face of the Bill, then we need more strength in this area.
When thinking of the target groups, I think particularly of the visible minorities and people who belong to ethnocultural communities. This is not necessarily always a matter of visibility in terms of colour or race. Visibility can be a matter of accents or features that strike an employer or personnel officer as being alien. Then, of course, there are the native people of Canada who are entering the cities in large numbers seeking employment. For that matter, they are seeking employment outside cities. The needs and concerns of the disabled and women have been addressed eloquently by other Members of the House. Surely a Government that states all the good intentions the Minister and her Parliamentary Secretary have declared should do something more with Clause 5 if it believes in those principles.
The flaws in Clause 5 are overwhelming. Where will the plans be kept? Will they be kept at the head offices of the companies? There is no obligation to tell anyone about the plans. In another clause, there is a provision for consultation with unions. How can there be consultation if the unions or whatever representatives the workers put forward do not have a right to see the plans?
Surely Conservative Members are not so naive that they think that leaving employment equity up to the good intentions of employers will work when we have had so much evidence of discriminatory practices in Toronto. The most shocking thing that those surveys of Toronto employment practices demonstrated was that there was widespread discrimination and that employers did not think that there was anything wrong with that. In that kind of a context, surely we need to lay the provisions on the employer. Surely there must be a requirement that the plans be public documents and be freely available to anyone who wants to look at them. Surely the community groups and those who have been frozen out by
Employment Equity
employers have the right of access to these plans if there is to be any kind of action taken on them.
I realize that I am drawing near the end of my time. In conclusion, I wish to say that I hope devoutly, with the entire depth of my being, that the Government will take this seriously and will take the Bill back to committee. Last Thursday I had a terribly depressing experience when, in one vote, we took care of 19 amendments to the Bill. The Government voted every one of them down.
It seems to me that the words which the then Opposition Leader and now Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in June, 1984 ring very hollow now. He said then that there is no obligation more compelling, no duty more irresistible, than to ensure that minorities live at all times in conditions of fairness and justice. Bill C-62 does not do that. It flouts the principles the Prime Minister stated before the last election.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question to ask of my colleague. Can my colleague possibly have any confidence that this legislation will bring about real change in the workplace and a greater equality between men and women in the workplace both in terms of the amount of money they earn and the positions they occupy given that there is presently great inequality and that companies have many other bases upon which to make their hiring decisions besides equity? Does my colleague have any confidence that this legislation will be a big enough stick to bring about the results that are so greatly needed today?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question asked by my colleague. The answer is certainly that I have no such confidence. I think of the situation in which would-be workers find themselves across the country. I have been focusing on Toronto because the Urban Alliance on Race Relations along with the Metropolitan Social Planning Council carried out the kinds of studies that were required there. These were quite imaginative studies which demonstrated the depth of racist and discriminatory practices in that city. I am sure Toronto is not unusual.
People want to work and they seek the reality of employment equity. My colleague alluded particularly to the matter of equal pay for work of equal value and the insurance that people who are hired are not discriminated against once they have been hired. Those other concerns do face us. This Bill does not provide any kind of sanction for that kind of action. It provides that a fine ought to be paid if reports are not made, but there is no provision for action on any of these matters. For a broken reed to be offered the people of Canada as a big stick is surely for us to be left with the gravest disappointment in what the Government claims to be doing.

Mr. Speaker, this Bill provides for a penalty of $50,000 if employers do not report on the level of employment equity in the workplace, yet many of the employers are very large firms and multinational corporations. I wonder if a fine of $50,000 would be effective if a very large firm simply

April 22, 1986
Employment Equity
decided to ignore the law and not collect the information necessary to comply with the minimal provisions of this legislation. I wonder if the legislation should not provide for a larger fine in order that it be enforceable.

Mr. Speaker, the matter of a $50,000 fine is worth some careful consideration. The cost of establishing an office to work toward employment equity in a company would, I suspect, on an annual basis, easily run to $100,000. The companies must employ officers with the kinds of skills required. I would expect that such a person would easily cost $35,000 or $40,000 per year. If one thinks of secretarial and other costs, I am sure it would exceed $50,000 in the way of costs. Surely to have a fine which is less than the cost of conforming to legislation is an open invitation to have it violated. If an employer saves money by paying a fine and being subjected to an employment inequity tax for a year as an alternative to employing people and establishing an office, I could imagine many cold-blooded employers saying: "Let's go ahead and pay the fine". It seems to me that that is a final declaration on the part of a Government which is not really serious about the matter.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with the point just made by the Hon. Member regarding the $50,000 fine for non-compliance. Both the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party attempted to get the Government to understand that $50,000 was not enough. We wanted $500,000 to be the fine for non-compliance. Does the Hon. Member not agree-and I think he alluded to it at the end of his remarks- that some employers will find it cheaper to pay the fine than to proceed with some important physical changes to their establishments to make them accessible to handicapped people? For example, I am referring to changes to their buildings so that handicapped people will have better access or so their establishments will be more secure and safe for those who may be blind, deaf, or whatever. I do not see any measure in the Bill for us to follow up on this with employers except to agree voluntarily that they will report on their plans after three years. Does he not agree that some companies will find it much easier to pay the $50,000 fine than to comply with sometimes expensive but needed changes to the systemic discrimination which is inherent in many workplaces today? For example, access to buildings can be difficult and there can be problems in terms of security and safety. Does he agree that perhaps it is merely symbolic to have a $50,000 fine for larger companies?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is absolutely right. At best the Bill will be a symbol. We have had a number of such symbols since the early 1980s with the establishment of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the work of several committees of the last Parliament. Given my particular responsibilities for multiculturalism in our caucus, I am keenly aware of the work of the special committee on the participation of visible minorities which made recommendations in these various areas. In early 1984, two
years ago, it declared the following in the title of its report Equality Now.
There were also reports dealing with the situation faced by disabled people, as another example. Whether or not the last Government was buying time in appointing Judge Rosalie Abella as a royal commissioner to investigate this area, I would not want to say just now. We are very grateful to her for having clarified for Canada what affirmative action could involve and the way in which we could make progress.
Given several advances over the last three years or so, there is a terrible responsibility on the shoulders of the Government to ensure that these beginnings continue. The Government should press for action so that these initiatives do not die as a result of half-hearted actions, whatever the protestations, which end up making people cynical about the stated principles. There is a terrible danger in that regard, and I see no readiness on the part of the Government to face up to that. If the Government accepts the motion and takes the matter back to committee, hopes would spring up somewhat.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate being given the floor at this time of day because I have several remarks to make on the motion before us.

And I would like to speak in support of the motion before the House, Mr. Speaker, namely, that:
"Bill C-62, An Act respecting employment equity, be not now read a third time, but that the Bill be referred back to a legislative committee for reconsideration of Clauses 3, 5 and 7 thereof'.
Mr. Speaker, I think that today we have heard some very positive comments on the measures proposed to achieve employment equity. I have never claimed, and neither has my colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine-East (Mr. Allmand) that everything has been done and all problems have been dealt with. Of course not. And I must say that the Bill before the House is a step, maybe not the giant step we would have liked, but at least a step. Not a particularly energetic one, because we are convinced that this Bill is a bit weak and that it would be a good idea for the Government to take it back and give it more teeth, more backbone, and it could then come back to the House with an amended Bill that would be much stronger, not just a Bill proposing something the House can agree with but that will never materialize.
Mr. Speaker, I would remind the House that the three clauses in question-

Clause 3 of Bill C-62 deals with interpretation. I should like to remind Hon. Members that the Opposition wanted to include federal Departments and agencies under the Act to ensure that the main employer in the Government, the Treasury Board, complied with the principles of employment equity and indeed provided an example for the private sector. We also proposed that persons who employ 25 people or more should be subject to the provisions of the Act rather than
April 22, 1986

employers of 100 or more as defined in the present state of the Bill. I will return to my point about federal Departments and agencies being included in the Bill, but first I want to make sure that I deal with these clauses in order.
Clause 5 refers to the action plans of companies setting out their goals and timetables. We think, in all honesty, that they should be made public. Why should they be hidden in the vaults of the head offices of national organizations? It could be difficult for someone in Vancouver to know exactly what is the action plan of a company which has its head office in Toronto. It may be hidden in a vault and may not be accessible to anyone who wanted to see it. We consider Clause 5 to be weak and would like to see it strengthened by making the action plans of employers public and by setting out goals and timetables so that all of us can see them.
Clause 7 refers to the famous fine of $50,000, which I think is a concession to non-action in the sense that it will not be enough to force companies to comply with the Bill. They will prefer to pay the $50,000 fine than to become involved in capital expenditures or capital works which may be required to eliminate systemic discrimination. We are talking about two very different things here. We are talking about discrimination as a matter of fact toward four target groups-women, native people, visible minorities, and the handicapped.
Also there is systemic discrimination which is inherent in the system, in the workplace, in our habits, and sometimes even in our thinking. We do not accept easily-by tradition, by lack of understanding and sometimes by ignorance-that some people with the capacity, the competence and the quality to serve the Canadian community cannot do so because of their status. As far as I am concerned, they are discriminated against by a system which is unresponsive and irresponsible with regard to their employment.
I want to come back to the first point.

I may say I have done a bit of research on the matter of the Government's obligation as an employer to be subject to the letter of the law and thus to Bill C-62. Mr. Speaker, I simply wish to recall, before making my specific comments on the Public Service and before saying why it should be included in the Bill, that yesterday in the House, that when I was listening to the Minister making the usual preliminary remarks at the third reading stage, and I quote,

At page 12452 of Hansard, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Ms. MacDonald) said:
I can say quite frankly that in the years before this Government came to power I heard a lot of talk about fairness and equality but I saw no action. What we are seeing here today is a Government committed to action in this field.
Here we have a responsible Minister telling us such things as that she has been here for 12 or 13 years and has heard a lot about fairness and equality but has seen no action. Where was
Employment Equity
the Minister in 1982 when the Charter of Rights was adopted? She saw action there. As a matter of fact I will remind her of what was said either by me or by somebody else in this House recently because it is worth repeating. Although I am not very proud of our record, I am not ashamed of it. There have been efforts. I must remind the House that measures were taken.
[Translation[
I would like to remind the House of the following facts, Mr. Speaker: In 1971, Canada was the first western country to recognize the role of women at the highest level of decisionmaking by creating a Cabinet position on the status of women, and I may add that I came to this House in 1972; in 1975, we had an omnibus Bill to ensure an equal status for women; in 1976, we passed the Canadian Human Rights Act which forbids discrimination based on sex; in 1978, we proposed changes to the Canada Pension Plan to provide for the equal sharing of retirement credits, as well as amendments to the Canada Labour Code to remove pregnancy as a motive for layoff or firing, and in 1982, we passed the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and I could continue.
We did take action, Mr. Speaker. We did not do enough to satisfy many people including your humble servant, but I still say that efforts were made and that we have to recognize this. However, it would be an exaggeration to say that nothing had been done before the Minister of Employment and Immigration was appointed, and I think that the Minister is too serious to suggest such a thing. The Hon. Members opposite should not always try to say that the Conservative Government has reinvented the wheel since the last election and they should stop bragging that nothing had been done before they came to power.
Things were done, Mr. Speaker, but it was not enough. As I have already said, Bill C-62 goes part of the way, but it is not strong enough; it lacks teeth. I would like to remind the House that the Abella Commission was created in 1983, only one year after the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms had been adopted. The Commission was created on June 24, 1983, under the chairmanship of Judge Rosalie Abella, and its report was tabled in this House on November 20, 1984.
If I may read the terms of reference of the Commission, it was asked to inquire "into the opportunities for employment of women, native people, disabled persons and visible minorities in certain Crown corporations and corporations wholly owned by the Government of Canada".
Mr. Speaker, employment equity means that no one should be refused a job for reasons which have nothing to do with his competence. It also means access to employment without any arbitrary obstacle, that is without discriminatory practices or attitudes which could hamper or even prevent access by individuals or groups to employment opportunities because of their particular characteristics, whether they be handicapped, women, native people or members of a visible minority. Indeed, for us, Frenchspeaking Canadians, Mr. Speaker, the native people are a visible minority. Thus we feel that three

April 22, 1986
Employment Equity
groups might have been enough. At any rate, my view is that there was no need to add that. Visible minorities in our minds are people who, like myself perhaps, have a face like mine with the nose in the wrong place, and, well, when one is born with this kind of face one has to live with it!
Mr. Speaker, the quest for employment equity must cut through all practices that discriminate against certain groups which have long been subject to such a discrimination. There must first be an effort towards identifying and eliminating discrimatory barriers. And when I speak of discrimatory barriers, it may be relevant to mention that where practices or systems are concerned, discrimatory barriers to employment do now exist. And our goal in the Official Opposition is to try and have the Government understand that Clauses 3, 5 and 7 must be redrawn to put teeth into the legislation.
As we know, Mr. Speaker, people are discriminated against for a number of reasons and in a number of ways. Some are discriminated against because of their economic or social conditions. Well, what do you expect? Others, for political reasons or because they lack education or vocational training. God knows that in her report, Judge Abella, if we care to read it, mentions this question of education, even referring to our landed immigrants who come here and speak neither English nor French, neither of our official languages, and who have difficulty in entering the labour market because they face discrimination for the very reason that they did not have a chance to learn one of this country's official languages. In the Abella Report, it is suggested that our whole language training system would need reviewing and I support Judge Abella's recommendations in that area-in order to eliminate one of the situations causing discrimination against new Canadians. It is subtle, sometimes persistent and it is pervasive. The fact is, it is systemic.
I would like to quote from page 10 of the report, concerning what Judge Abella views as systemic discrimination.
Systemic discrimination requires systemic remedies. Rather than approaching discrimination from the perspective of the single perpetrator and the single victim, the systemic approach acknowledges that by and large the systems and practices we customarily and often unwittingly adopt may have an unjustifiably negative effect on certain groups in society.
The effect of the system on the individual or group, rather than its attitudinal sources, governs whether or not a remedy is justified.
Remedial measures of a systemic and systematic kind are the object of employment equity and affirmative action. They are meant to improve the situation for individuals who, by virtue of belonging to and being identified with a particular group, find themselves unfairly and adversely affected by certain systems or practices.
Mr. Speaker, it could not be said any better. Judge Abella has described this quite well, and I agree with her.
During the remaining minutes, I should like to deal briefly with a problem which concerns a great many people in the Ottawa-Vanier and Ottawa-Carleton regions. I refer-to the issue of applying this Bill to the main employer and the Federal departments.
I want to do this because in a press release dated March 8, 1985, dealing with employment equity in the Federal Public Service, I read: "The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de
Cotret) announced today the various steps which the Government intends to take within the Federal Public Service and Crown Corporations to achieve employment equity for women, the natives, the handicapped and the members of visible minorities".
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, this is quite relevant to Bill C-62.
The measures announced are as follows: to reinforce the federal Government's Affirmative Action Program announced in June 1983, to which I referred earlier, and will include an immediate review by Treasury Board to detect any systemic barriers that may exist in the classification system for senior positions. I repeat: any systemic barriers that may exist in the classification system.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, the classification of a position depends on the number of points it is given, and the salary in turn depends on the classification. A definition of the word "classification" is given in the Treasury Board and Public Service Glossary: "Classification of Positions-Method for defining a job by category and occupational group and for evaluating the job and assigning it to a level within the group."
Mr. Speaker, this is a way to identify the relative value of jobs. Heaven knows we urgently need a thorough study of the situation and an answer to the classification problem!
In the 1984 election campaign, members of the Progressive Conservative Party told public servants: We will put job classification on the bargaining table. Everybody said it was a good idea. And then they said: We are going to do a study. And they did. And not long ago, when I asked how the classification study was progressing, the answer was: The study made by Treasury Board was finished today, but a second study Treasury Board had done by Thorne, Stevenson and Kellogg and which I am told has been completed, has been submitted to the Ministers responsible for Treasury Board, for study and consideration.
Mr. Speaker, it is now April 22, 1986. This Government was elected a year and one-half or more ago, and we are still at the study stage, trying to find out what systemic classification is and what the possible barriers are.
Mr. Speaker, I would like the Government to tell us what is going to happen with position classification, so public servants will know exactly what is being done about this problem. In the classification process, the person who does the classifying decides how the position is rated and what the employee is going to earn. And these are very important points for public servants. They want to negotiate the classification of a position. They want to know the classification criteria and want to sit down at the bargaining table and say: We think the system should be improved. We think there are obstacles in this system which sometimes discriminate against certain people, and we want to correct that. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, ours is a reasonable position. Since the Government made that an election promise, it should at least keep its word on this and give public servants
April 22, 1986

the advantage of being able to negotiate job classifications in the near future.
In the same March 8, 1985 statement, Mr. Speaker, the President of the Treasury Board talked about the immediate establishment of a Treasury Board review process to uncover any systemic obstacles, and about greater emphasis on strategies aimed at implementing specific affirmative action plans related to results in the various departments.
Mr. Speaker, I asked the question: Where are these plans? I was told today that 41 strategy plans are available directly from the departments. Three departments have failed to produce their plans. We will see. I asked whether they were available to the public, and I was told it would take a truck to transport them. Can somebody on the Government side tell us why the affirmative action plans in the departments... Perhaps somebody might tell us what this is all about. Are they satisfactory? Have they been assessed? Has anything been done as a result of this important affirmative action initiative?
Then, Mr. Speaker, in the same press release the President of the Treasury Board states: "The unions will be invited to sit on a committee dealing with the equal pay for equal work issue."
Mr. Speaker, I am all for it. And I think every Member of this House will agree. That is why we should go back to the Committee and listen to what the President of Treasury Board has to say about this action plan to implement equal pay for equal work or work of equal value policy. I know that thirteen unions are having meetings with the Treasury Board representative every two months, and that a report is to be submitted by March 1987.
Mr. Speaker, I will therefore have to wait another year to find out what is happening, and they want us to adopt a Bill that has no teeth, and which I find is totally unsuited to meeting this challenge, a Bill that systematically excludes Government departments. The latter are hesitant and have yet to explain to me, as a politician, what has been done about job classification affirmative action and in the departments and how the committees that are supposed to work out a plan for equal pay for equal work or work of equal value are progressing.
Mr. Speaker, it all boils down to the fact that I think referring all this to committee for study and consideration is a reasonable suggestion, and I hope the House will decide this is the right thing to do. I hope I can come back at a subsequent stage to continue my remarks.

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment on some of the statements the Member made, and I have a question for him as well. There was debate earlier this afternoon dealing with the strength or weakness of provisions for affirmative action in the Province of Saskatchewan. I note
Employment Equity
that under the previous New Democratic Government in Saskatchewan affirmative action provisions were implemented for Crown corporations, particularly in northern Saskatchewan. Progress had been made.
I have a report of a human rights consultant to the Department of the Secretary of State. The report notes that when the Conservative Government came into power in Saskatchewan it made the policy voluntary for Crown corporations. The consultant notes that the respondents are discovering that these affirmative action plans are in no way entrenched within the employment systems of all the Crown corporations. With the change in Government, the political commitment has waned. Each Crown corporation now decides its own policy, with the result that the program has become fragmented and dependent upon the particular commitment of the individual corporation. The report indicates that the respondents have concluded that the weakness of their strategy lies in its voluntary nature.
To what extent does the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) feel that Bill C-62 reflects a similar turn by the federal Conservative Government to a voluntary approach? How dramatically does he think the Bill will fail in achieving employment equity?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order to do justice to that rather important question, I invite the Member to read some of the speeches that I have made in the last while on this Bill. In the last election campaign in Manitoba all Parties paid homage to employment equity and said that they would commit themselves to that program. I take it that Manitoba was moving in that direction. I am told by my colleague, the Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), that in Saskatchewan only five Crown corporations have an affirmative action program. According to press reports, the Government is cutting funds to these companies and there is also a hiring freeze. The present Government is not, therefore, as enthusiastic as the previous Government was. Let us hope that it comes to its senses. We are told not to believe everything we read, but from press releases I understand that some actions were being taken in Saskatchewan with regard to employment equity.
British Columbia has yet to come up with employment equity legislation. My research does not show the existence of any such legislation in B.C. at all. We are hoping that a more sensitive and sensible Government will come into power there some day and bring some equity to employment practices.
[DOT] (noo)
I call this the smoke and mirrors Bill. That is the title I put on my copy. It reflects what we all like but it does not do much in the way of action. Despite the fact that the Minister spent quite some time yesterday telling us how she was committed to action on employment equity, I fail to see in this Bill any real action. I invite the Hon. Member to read some of the comments we have made regarding the improvements to the Bill through the 20-odd amendments we tried to get through. They

April 22, 1986
Employment Equity
were all turned down by the Government because Members opposite do not like constructive and worth-while amendments to their legislation. They feel it is sacred and therefore untouchable. I disagree. This House should have more understanding of the issues and should debate them a little longer. That is why I want the Bill to go back to committee.
Any further questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be recognized in order to say a few words at this stage of the deliberations on Bill C-62, dealing with employment equity. As my friend just indicated, it should be called a smoke and mirrors Bill, or a fluff and puff Bill, or a magician's Bill. Now you see it, now you don't.
In my deliberations with friends and colleagues across the country there seemed to be the impression that the Government is acting on employment equity to some extent. The important words there are "to some extent". It is a minute step in the right direction on a very long and difficult road. In one sense it does more damage than good in that it gives the impression that employment equity is finally being recognized. Finally we are going to do something to help the disabled, native people, women and visible minorities to experience equality and equity in the workplace.
Unfortunately, those who are knowledgeable about this subject, those who possess expertise, those who have studied the issue, or those who are representative of the various groups this Bill is directed towards, have a certain uniform reaction to the Bill. That reaction is that it is not adequate. It fails to meet the purpose of the Bill. It is not surprising that people have been misled a little when you read the purpose of the Bill. It says:
The purpose of this Act is to achieve equality in the work place so that no person shall be denied employment opportunities or benefits for reasons unrelated to ability and, in the fulfilment of that goal, to correct the conditions of disadvantage in employment experienced by women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and persons who are, because of their race or colour, in a visible minority in Canada by giving effect to the principle that employment equity means more than treating persons in the same way but also requires special measures and the accommodation of differences.
We have no concern regarding that purpose as stated. The point is that the Bill does not do any of that. It fails to meet this purpose, this goal, this objective. It falls far short. I am sure you would take my word for it but you do not have to. You can take the word of Suzanne Boivin of the National Association of Women and the Law. She says:
Nothing will change. Unfortunately, it is simply wishful thinking.
The Inuit of Canada say that, for aboriginal peoples:
Bill C-62 is of limited value.
Beryl Potter of the Coalition on Employment Equity for Disabled Persons had this to say:
Like the Bill-it's not even worth the paper it's written on-I've never been so disillusioned in my life as I am with Prime Minister Mulroney.
I was a supporter of him. I worked for him in his campaign and I am totally, totally disillusioned.
Here are perhaps the most knowledgeable people in Canada on this issue commenting on Bill C-62 and they say it is inadequate, incomplete, inappropriate, wishful thinking, and will simply not do the job it sets out to do.
I will not read the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on this issue in the election campaign of 1984.1 do not think it does him justice to point out what he said in that campaign regarding bringing in all sorts of employment equity initiatives to ensure there would be no discrimination in the workplace, to ensure there would be encouragement and support of strategies for native people, visible minorities, the disabled, and women. He has failed to deliver. I would not want to spend too much time pointing that out because I suspect everyone is well aware of it anyway.
The purpose of the Bill is primarily to prevent employment practices which act as barriers to employment for some very specific groups such as women, the disabled, native people and visible minorities. In a previous career I had an opportunity to work with the disabled, young native people, and those who would be classified as visible minorities in an attempt to find employment opportunities for them. I suppose I should include women in that as well, but my main experience was with those groups I mentioned. Of course they all included women. That was not many years ago. When I identified a workplace for someone among these groups, my job was to send that person down to the place concerned for employment experience of one kind or another, on-the-job training in a sense. I am afraid I have to say that when the employer found that the individual was not a white Anglo-Saxon, but rather someone from a visible minority, he or she inevitably found a reason to cancel the job training opportunity. I could present literally hundreds of names of individuals for whom I found a job opportunity, without mentioning the fact that they were, let us say, a native youngster, and when that individual showed up they were inevitably turned away. Then we went through that process the next day and the same people would be turned away again. Yet, when they phoned me they would inevitably say, "Mr. Riis, I am not prejudiced. I don't discriminate against people but I really cannot afford to hire a native person", or someone who was disabled, or a member of a certain ethnic group. Quite frankly, that is a racist attitude. It is discrimination. It indicates prejudice. Therefore, when I look at the provisions in this Bill and see what it is attempting to accomplish, it hits very close to my heart. It reminds me of a very close personal experience that occurred to me for a number of years. It was an embarrassment to me as a Canadian citizen that in spite of all the glorious comments about being tolerant, open minded, non-discriminatory, liberal and progressive in our thinking, when push came to shove almost inevitably that discrimination existed in the workplace.
I was encouraged when I heard in the post-election period that the Government would introduce a Bill that would finally bring about employment equity in Canada through a program to encourage employers to hire native people, the disabled,
April 22, 1986

visual minorities and women. However, once one had an opportunity to examine this Bill and hear the witnesses who came to speak to the committee about this Bill, it became obvious that it was rife with flaws and filled with inconsistencies. It was simply an inappropriate piece of legislation.
One might ask why it is inappropriate. One of the shortcomings is that there is no mandatory equity, no enforcement and no real penalties. This legislation must be viewed as voluntary equity with mandatory reporting of workforce data. Those businesses over a certain size that carry out transactions with the federal Government over a certain amount must submit an action program. So what? Big deal. Although the employer must draft an action plan, there is no requirement that the employer must fulfil that plan or necessarily introduce it. However, there is a penalty pursuant to Clause 6, with a maximum summary conviction of $50,000, if the employer fails to act.
We in the New Democratic Party attempted to make this penalty realistic. Heather Reisman, who works with the Nesbitt Consulting Group which provides advice to these firms which are interested or essentially forced to introduce a program of equity in the workplace on paper, said about the penalty: "It's squat". The effectiveness of the maximum $50,000 fine for failing to report workforce data annually is something that she says a large company will simply write off as a cost of doing business. Fifty thousand dollars is irrelevant to a corporation of the size essentially contemplated by this Bill. She says that it is "squat". There really is no effective penalty for making no progress. It is somewhat Pollyannish and naive to believe that employers throughout Canada will implement equity programs for their employers that will require them to hire people whom obviously they are not interested in hiring. Nevertheless, that is the purpose of this Bill.
The target groups who appeared before the committee made it clear that a firm must be obliged to develop an action plan with goals and timetables, including how it will remove discriminatory practices, and take the positive steps needed to bring about employment equity.
These action plans were not included in the original Bill. Indeed, the Minister claimed before the committee that an action plan was inherent for the company introducing equity. In a sense, the Government itself did not consider that an action plan ought to be part of the Bill. It is an example of how this Bill has not been clearly thought through and needs to go back to committee for reconsideration. After all, we are theoretically launching a major new initiative for Canada. We are giving the impression that employment equity will become a reality in our country, but the fact is that it will not happen.
When one considers the importance of this Bill and the success of a similar Bill in the United States, we should be taking much more time to ensure that this is a good Bill that employers and employees from all parts of Canada will support. While some enforcement is needed, in order for these legislative requirements to work it is necessary to have the
Employment Equity
general support of the people. The fact is that the initiatives in Bill C-62 simply will not accomplish that.
I want to comment on equal pay for work of equal value. On many occasions members of the Government turned aside attempts to include in the Bill a reference to equal pay for work of equal value. The National Action Committee on the Status of Women urged that this Bill contain a reference to Section 11 of the Canadian Human Rights Act so that the equal pay matter could be addressed by employers. We attempted to introduce that equal pay provision without success. The Government argued time and again that the presence of equal pay in the Canadian Human Rights Act as it stands is good enough. However, that is not the case.
Judge Rosalie Abella is perhaps one of the most knowledgeable people in this area. She stated in her landmark study that equal pay is an integral element in the implementation of employment equity and that it must be included in any undertaking by employers to make the practices in the workplace more equitable. I suggest that the most knowledgeable person in the land sums it up very well when she says that we must include these provisions in the Act if we are serious about equal pay for work of equal value.
The clause on contract compliance is a major weakness in the Bill. I would remind the House that in 1980, the Canadian Government had contracts with some 25,000 firms in Canada; $6.5 billion worth of private sector business and some $5.5 billion of business to Crown corporations.
In 1982-83, the Department of Supply and Services alone signed with federal firms literally over 333,000 contracts worth $5 billion. Such a major undertaking in terms of Government business begs the question: What is the nature of the Government's contract compliance policy? It applies only to firms with 100 or more employees and only if the value of the contract exceeds $200,000. The only obligation on the contractor is simply to implement equity in the workplace. Failure to do so does not mean a loss of a contract, although such firm may be removed from the competition for future contracts. The firm "may" be removed.
There is either a commitment in law or there is not. The fact that a company may not do further business with the Government if it does not comply indicates that this is a rather limp wristed, milque-toast approach to the whole matter.
The Government's compliance policy does not require a contractor to file a report on workforce data as is required by those firms that come under Bill C-62.
These are hardly owners' requirements and certainly are far inferior to the demands made upon firms contracting in the United States. The approach in the United States is quite different and much more serious than the one reflected in Bill C-62.
In conclusion let me say that our Party has five concerns. First, there is the absence of real enforcement and adequate penalties under mandatory equity schemes. Second, there is no

April 22, 1986
Employment Equity
reference in the Bill to equal pay for work of equal value. Third, no contract compliance is included. Fourth, there is no obligation to negotiate equity where there is a bargaining unit. Perhaps, most important, the coverage of the Bill is inadequate in that it does not include federal Departments. If we are serious about asking people to take this Bill seriously, then surely its provisions should be extended to include those people, including federal Departments.
Are there questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand).

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the Hon. Member's remarks about his own experience with designated groups, I presume in British Columbia, and his attempts to find work for them. He mentioned the fact that sometimes they ran up against this systemic discrimination. Based on the Hon. Member's experience, what does he think about the attempt to deal with this matter through voluntary enforcement? We have said all along that the Bill is not an enforceable employment equity Bill. It is a Bill which provides information about different workplaces. That information is to be made public in the hope that the public will comment on what is happening and, through public opinion, force employment equity. The Government is committed to ensuring that employment equity becomes a reality. We intend to knock on the doors of employers who do not meet their responsibilities. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that we will be knocking with a firm fist.

What they should be able to do is lay a charge. The charge would go to a court and the court would say whether or not employment equity was being implemented.
So she admits in her speech that this is not really an enforceable employment equity Bill. It is one in which, through the publication of information, the Government hopes that there will be voluntary compliance. Can the Hon. Member tell us from his experience with what he was trying to do in British Columbia whether that really worked? Or do we need Bills with teeth in them under which charges can be laid and offenders prosecuted when there is not the employment equity which we all seek?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his thoughtful question. No, I do not think for a moment that voluntary compliance will work. I think that a Bill without teeth is simply not worth the paper upon which it is written. Quite frankly, I do not want to be part of any Bill which requires the poor Minister responsible to go out across Canada banging on doors. I hope she has something better to do with her time. If she is serious about providing employment

subtopic: NATIVE ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT FUND-EXTENT OF EXPENDITURES. (B) REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Would Hon. Members either sit down and listen to the great speech which the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) is going to make, or leave the Chamber.

subtopic: NATIVE ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT FUND-EXTENT OF EXPENDITURES. (B) REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I draw to the attention of the House that under the previous administration, a $345 million native economic development program was established. That amount was to be expended over a four-year period, beginning in April of 1984. The purpose of the program was to enable native people to break free of their dependency on social assistance. It was to create among native people an entrepreneurial group who would be economically self-sufficient in time and then become employers of other native people. The program was directed at the development of native-owned businesses, including individual entrepreneurs, corporations, and community-based businesses.
I would like to remind the House that in their struggle to have aboriginal rights recognized and implemented, native people have had to focus an inordinate amount of time on the political process. As a result, there are a large number of very competent, articulate and successful political leaders in the native community. As a matter of fact, we in this House of Commons could learn a lot about political leadership by looking at the very able political leaders in the native community and recognizing their talents and skills. They have begun to see that the judicial route is a promising avenue for some degree of redress of grievances over long-standing historical injustices.
An increasing number of native people are turning to the study of law as a result. Their accomplishments in that field are many. However, it is in the field of economic development where bold new action is required. Hence the reason for the native economic development program. It was designed to help native people break through the poverty barrier and open the way for full participation in the business life of this nation.
My concern is that I detect a distinct lack of commitment by this Government to that avenue of endeavour. My evidence is no less a source than that despised Nielsen task force report on natives and Indians, the so-called Buffalo Jump Report. On page 68 it says that although halfway through its mandate the native economic development program has approved only 34 projects at a total cost of $11.7 million, 21 additional projects have been recommended for approval. In the year 1985-86, $122.1 million was approved by Parliament with a strong Conservative majority. Nevertheless, in the last fiscal year the Minister allowed $90 million of that to lapse. It seems to me the Government wants to bury the native economic development program. I find it difficult to blame the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Bissonnette) because I know that his orders come from the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens). Having been associated with that Minister for a long time, we know his ultra-conservative and archaic philosophy could never support such a program. We also know that the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) is no friend and ally of the native economic development program. In fact, he

April 22, 1986
Adjournment Debate
was instrumental in having turned down the very promising Yukon Indian Development Corporation project.
I conclude very simply and quickly by asking why the Government does not admit that it wants to kill this program just as it did Katimavik? Why not be forthright and say so? Do not let the native people of this country go on believing there is such a program when it does not exist. So far there have been 900 proposals under this program. The applicants have been disappointed and frustrated by delays, postponements and, finally, turn-downs in most cases. Economic development is not a priority with the Department of Indian Affairs. Only 4 per cent of its budget is directed to that avenue, and most of that money is diverted elsewhere. Therefore, we need the native economic development program. The Government has failed to recognize that, failed to respond to it, and I argue that in doing so it has made a gross error.

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Bissonnette (Minister of State (Small Businesses)):
subtopic: NATIVE ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT FUND-EXTENT OF EXPENDITURES. (B) REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address the question raised by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) concerning the Native Economic Development Program.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, contrary to what the Hon. Member just said, I was given responsibility for this program by the Prime Minister, and never have the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) and the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) interfered with the way the program was managed. First of all, I can give the House the assurance that the Conservative Government is working very hard to safeguard the economic and social interests of Canada's native peoples. The native community is aware of the Native Economic Development Program and it uses it. This is borne out by the fact that more than 900 project applications were submitted, and out of that number, unlike the erroneous figures you had, 145 were approved, representing a value of $59.3 million. The program is very popular with our native people, no doubt about that.
Mr. Speaker, the NEDP which is aimed at helping native people achieve economic independence is administered by the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion but directed by the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Bissonnette), and has a budget of $345 million spread out over a period of four years, starting in 1984-85. This funding has not been affected by budgetary cutbacks. The NEDP plays a very important role in native economic development. It is the only program that is specifically aimed at developing the economic independence of native people.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Hon. Member would feel better if he met with representatives of the following organizations: the Central Interior Trust Company in Kamloops, British Columbia, which received a contribution of $6.9 million; the Saskatchewan Indian Loan Company, which received a contribution of $2.6 million, and so forth. It has been estimated
that this $2.6 billion federal contribution to the Saskatchewan Indian Loan Company would generate more than $46 million of new investments in the provincial agricultural economy. The same might be said about the Association of Reserves for Improving Social Economics which was given $1.3 million. Thanks to this contribution, it is expected that 100 new businesses and 400 new permanent jobs will be created in the next few years.
Mr. Speaker, these propositions are perfect examples of the dynamic and creative force of native people. They also emphasize the importance of the program's effective assistance to the native people of Canada.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would say to the Liberal Member that he is quite misinformed, and that the native people are pleased to work with the department and the Minister of State for Small Businesses to improve the program.

subtopic: MULTICULTURALISM-WHITE PAPER INQUIRY. (B) REQUEST FOR CONSULTATIONS
MULTICULTURALISM-WHITE PAPER INQUIRY. (B) REQUEST FOR CONSULTATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 18, I addressed several questions to the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Jelinek). These questions reflected my understanding that the multiculturalism sector was working on a White Paper on multicultural policy but that this work had been given up under the instructions of the Minister. The answers that I received did not really clarify that question, and that is why I asked to have a further opportunity to debate the matter.
Now, more than five months later, it is even more appropriate to ask what the Government's multiculturalism policy is. On March 7, less than four months after the Minister's statement that there would be full consultation, particularly with the new Standing Committee on Multiculturalism, it was reported in The Globe and Mail that he was in fact involved in creating a totally new multiculturalism policy.
Those are the words of the Minister aimed at bringing ethnic minorities out of, as he said, "ethno-cultural corners" and into the economic mainstream of Canada. He declared that the policy was in the final stages of preparation for Cabinet. He then went on to suggest, without any doubt about what the result would be, that he was not going to Cabinet for additional funds. Given that he was talking about re-orienting spending, he said that it would be a redirection of existing funds. There is no doubt that some organizations will be cut out. He went on to say that the organizations might be involved in the retention of culture and that henceforth there was no question that their grants would have to be an investment in Canada. He concluded by stating:
"We're not going to be spoon-feeding these people, giving them grants or financial assistance or any form of assistance-What we have to do is open the doors and give them an opportunity to get involved instead of having a multiculturalism conference and talking about various cultures".
April 22, 1986

That statement has been taken by ethno-cultural, multicultural, race relations, immigrant settlement and other organizations as just short of a declaration of war by the Minister of State for Multiculturalism against their intentions. Across the country there is the most intense unease about what the Minister has in mind. Thus I address this question.
Surely what was needed was a White Paper on multiculturalism in the terms suggested in my question of November 18. Surely it was necessary for the intentions of the Minister to be laid out. It is necessary for him to turn back to the ethnocultural communities, since he clarified a need for redirection, in order to publish a paper to which they can react.
Some of the strongest reactions to this move have come from groups in the Province of Manitoba. They feel left out of the process. They feel neglected and rejected by the Minister. Two days before I asked this question in the House he met with executive members of the Manitoba Intercultural Council. He promised them there would be no change in multicultural policy without full consultation. People who recently had the pleasure of having a Manitoba Member of Parliament as Minister of State for Multiculturalism had been promised that regional priorities and regional concerns would be reflected upon by the Government as it dealt with these matters. They were promised that there would be full consultation.
It is not surprising that in Manitoba and in Alberta there is unease with what is happening. I spoke to a leader of the Urkrainian-Canadian community in Alberta late last week and he expressed his unease. He was convinced that this was a play to the City of Toronto and groups in Toronto, particularly to business groups. The most reassuring thing I could tell him was that when I was in attendance at the Multiculturalism Means Business Conference in Toronto, it was patently obvious that the policy shift suggested by the Minister on March 7 is not acceptable to large numbers of people. We might think that the first concern would be with respect to those organizations involved with multicultural retention. In many cases, those might be groups of European origin.
I was impressed that the questions asked of the Minister and of the panelists came as much from those we would think of as visible minority groups, groups which are surely concerned about race relation matters, employment equity, and matters as diverse as immigrant settlement and the establishment of credentials for those who have been trained outside Canada. These people are convinced that the Minister may forget their needs and not fund them adequately. They deeply resent the suggestion that he has been spoon-feeding them when, in fact, they have received precious little money. They now see the limited funds upon which they have depended in the past to stimulate their efforts being lost to them as the Government turns to other business-oriented efforts.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-INCORRECT REPORTING OF GAS PRICES ALLEGED
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-INCORRECT REPORTING OF GAS PRICES ALLEGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I recently asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of

April 22, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Communications (Mr. Edwards) a question concerning the need to ensure that the CBC reports to Canadians in an unbiased and balanced manner. The particular example I cited was from The Journal of March 7, 1986, in which a reporter doing a story about gas prices in Canada and the United States neglected to convert American dollars to Canadian dollars and American gallons to litres. Of course, this resulted in a very inaccurate statement of the comparison between Canadian and American gas prices. This is but one example of inaccurate and biased reporting by the CBC.
I have had some correspondence with Mr. David Spanjer of Elliotwood Court in my riding of Don Valley East. Mr. Spanjer has devoted much time to analysing the content of CBC Radio programming, and he feels that the coverage provided is not balanced. In a letter to me, he describes travelling by car through northern Ontario and how the reception from the CBC comes through loud and clear when all other stations have faded. He wrote:
I have no quarrel with this if the reporting of the news, the choice of the discussion subjects and the selection of the persons interviewed was objective. Unfortunately, exactly the opposite is the case-
Mr. Spanjer has written to the CBC on several occasions and has been very frustrated by the response he has received. Also he wrote:
As a taxpayer I believe I have the right to response to any reasonable request for information and a reply to any complaint that is properly documented. What in fact has happened is that the CBC has stalled for almost a year. They have refused to provide all the information requested . .. and now, rather than reply to my analysis of the program information that I received, they have arbitrarily declared the matter closed.
This is no way for a publicly owned corporation to treat one of its consumers and in effect one of its shareholders.
The Parliamentary Secretary in his response to my question pointed out that programming and content were the direct responsibility of CBC management and its Board of Directors. I appreciate the independence of the CBC and the need for its independence. However, it is no justification for inaccurate and biased reporting. This is clearly unacceptable to most Canadians.
On April 3, the President of the CBC, Pierre Juneau, announced the following:
Although the CBC received an increase in its parliamentary appropriations and although the corporation anticipates an increase in advertising revenue, this still leaves the CBC with a $48 million shortfall in 1986-87.
He went on to say that the shortfall resulted from the financial impacts of government cost-cutting measures and general economic factors, such as inflation and the devalued Canadian dollar, increasing the cost of goods and programming from outside Canada. He continued:
This year the corporation has not been able to avoid cuts in programming. Even the reductions in administrative and support expenditures will have an impact on programming and distribution services.
The CBC will eliminate 122 hours of network TV programming-77 hours of English language TV and 45 hours of
French language TV. Several programs, such as This Land and CBLT Morning in Toronto, have been dropped. Others have had their schedules curtailed.
In the April 14 issue of Maclean's magazine, an article dealing with CBC cut-backs indicated that officials at both the Treasury Board and the Department of Communications had calculated that in fact the CBC would have a deficit of less than $10 million in 1986-87 rather than the $48 million shortfall reported by Mr. Juneau. The article in Macleans also indicated that the CBC earned more than $33 million in unexpected advertising revenue in 1985-86 which the corporation was permitted to keep. The article also pointed out that the Government was giving the corporation an increase of $22 million or 2.1 per cent for 1986-87 operations and capital expenditures. The Main Estimates of the Government predict a $55 million increase in CBC advertising revenue.
In terms of advertising revenue, the CBC expects an increase of only $8 million over the 1984-85 actual revenue and only marginal increases for 1986-87 due to increased competition in several Canadian markets. Perhaps that sends out a message about the quality of programming. In addition, interesting and important questions were raised in the Maclean's article and in the CBC's own response about the corporation's budget, accounting practices, and ability to live within its means.
In the same week that the programming cuts and elimination of jobs were announced, Mr. Juneau and three senior Vice-Presidents departed on a 10-day trip to China to explore the potential for an export market for Canadian programming. This effort to sell Canadian programming abroad is hardly consistent with the cut-backs in Canadian programming. Not only are examples cited of biased and inaccurate reporting, but of biased and inappropriate spending practices as well.
Cut-backs of any sort are difficult. I have had that experience in my own business career. However, it appears that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation needs to re-examine its priorities in terms of its mandate. It needs to get at the structure, the number of senior vice-presidents, the number of vice-presidents and perhaps even to merge departments. The provision of balanced and accurate news and original Canadian programming is a vital duty of the CBC. It should also be managed according to sound business principles and practices.
I would ask my colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications (Mr. Edwards), to share these real concerns with the management and directors of the CBC on behalf of myself, my constituents and, I am sure, I am speaking for hundreds of thousands of Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-INCORRECT REPORTING OF GAS PRICES ALLEGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue of balanced coverage in our broadcast media is important to all Canadians. The free flow of information is vital to the functioning of
April 22, 1986

democracy. I can well appreciate, therefore, the Hon. Member's concern about the item on gas prices broadcast by the CBC which was aired on The National on March 7.
As I stated on March 21, broadcasters themselves are responsible for program selection and content, subject to the general rules and regulations of the CRTC. Thus responsibility for CBC programming matters lies entirely with the CBC's management and board of directors. I assured the House when the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) brought this matter to our attention that the CBC would be informed of his concern, and the corporation has since issued a response. I will be forwarding to the Hon. Member a copy of the full text of that response, but I would like at this time, with your permission, Sir, to provide a brief summary of it.
According to the CBC, the report in question was reviewed by senior TV news personnel and they found it to be fair and balanced over all. However, the CBC acknowledges a factual error in the comparison the Canadian pump price of gasoline with the American pump price in that the news item erroneously compared 95 cents per gallon U.S. with 20 cents Canadian per litre without adjustment for the U.S. exchange rate on the U.S. gallon. The CBC expresses its regret for these two errors.
The CBC has an internationally recognized reputation for the quality of its news and public affairs reporting. I can say with some knowledge, Sir, as a former broadcaster that
Adjournment Debate
omissions can occur in the reporting of information, particularly in the television medium where deadlines are often tight and a strict economy of time must be observed.
Parliament recognized when the Broadcasting Act was passed in 1968 that while programming autonomy must be assured, broadcasters must also assume certain responsibilities in conveying the information they broadcast. That is why Section 3(g) of the Act, which sets out CBC's mandate, begins by stating that the CBC should:
-be a balanced service of information, enlightenment and entertainment for people of different ages, interests and tastes covering the whole range of programming in fair proportion.

I am certain, Mr. Speaker, that these provisions of the Broadcasting Act have proven generally very useful and that the broadcasters have faithfully lived up to their responsibilities.
The Corporation has examined this report and prepared a detailed answer in which it recognizes the mistake and expresses its regret. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the reply of the CBC in this case shows how conscienciously the Corporation takes its responsibilities as a public broadcaster.
